preview.text: Some startups spend heavily and delay profit so they can grow quickly. This creates a difficult choice between speed and financial discipline. Understanding this issue can help you judge startup strategies more carefully. As you listen, ask: under what conditions can growth before profit be a reasonable strategy?

full_story_part1.text: For some startups, profit is not the first finish line. They spend heavily to gain users, enter markets, and grow faster than competitors. This can look dangerous. But when a company has a real network effect, speed may have a clear economic purpose. Research by Michael Katz and Carl Shapiro in 1985 explained the basic idea. A product may become more valuable to each user as more people use it. That can start a powerful cycle. More users create more value. More value attracts more users. An early lead may then build into a lasting advantage. In these markets, even the product with the best technology does not always win. Starting late can become a growing problem.

full_story_part1.canonical_text:
For some startups, profit is not the first finish line.

They spend heavily to gain users, enter markets, and grow faster than competitors. This can look dangerous. But when a company has a real network effect, speed may have a clear economic purpose.

Research by Michael Katz and Carl Shapiro in 1985 explained the basic idea. A product may become more valuable to each user as more people use it.

That can start a powerful cycle.

More users create more value. More value attracts more users. An early lead may then build into a lasting advantage. In these markets, even the product with the best technology does not always win. Starting late can become a growing problem.

full_story_part2.text: Pete Flint of NFX argued in 2020 that companies with genuine network effects may have good reasons to choose growth before profit. Some markets can become winner-take-most races. After reaching critical mass, a company may also have a chance to move from losses to profit. But there is a trap hidden inside the word growth. A rising customer count does not prove that a strong network is forming. NFX presents Groupon as a warning. Its fast expansion hid the loss of merchants and sellers that could not be sustained. The article also points to some direct-to-consumer companies in mattresses, shoes, and meal kits. They used blitzscaling-style growth without strong network effects or other clear defenses. Several later faced lower-value funding rounds and investor losses. In other words, speed can build a fortress—or simply make a weak business burn money faster.

full_story_part2.canonical_text:
Pete Flint of NFX argued in 2020 that companies with genuine network effects may have good reasons to choose growth before profit. Some markets can become “winner-take-most” races. After reaching critical mass, a company may also have a chance to move from losses to profit.

But there is a trap hidden inside the word “growth.”

A rising customer count does not prove that a strong network is forming. NFX presents Groupon as a warning. Its fast expansion hid the loss of merchants and sellers that could not be sustained.

The article also points to some direct-to-consumer companies in mattresses, shoes, and meal kits. They used blitzscaling-style growth without strong network effects or other clear defenses. Several later faced lower-value funding rounds and investor losses.

In other words, speed can build a fortress—or simply make a weak business burn money faster.

point_one.text: NFX suggests annual growth of 3 to 5 times after product-market fit at the Seed or Series A stage. Later, growth should work together with efficient customer acquisition. Useful checks include the Rule of 40 and recovering customer acquisition costs within about 3 to 6 months.

point_two.text: NFX notes that private equity acquisitions rose from 4% of relevant transactions in 2008 to 11% in 2019. This does not prove a complete return to profit, but it signals greater interest in efficiency. A 2020 *Business Horizons* paper by Kuratko, Holt, and Neubert also critically examined blitzscaling.
